title: Bollinger v. Central Pennsylvania Quarry Stripping and Construction Co.
summary: Proof of a shared drafting omission supported reformation of the writing to include the promised restoration of topsoil.
notes: 425 Pa. 430, 229 A.2d 741 (1967). The Bollingers' failure to read the writing before signing did not bar reformation once mutual mistake was shown; the contractor's own initial compliance with the topsoil procedure was key corroboration.

sections.Parties: Mahlon and Vinetta Bollinger sought to reform and enforce their agreement with the contractor depositing construction waste on their property.
sections.Material Facts:
The written agreement permitted the contractor to deposit waste from nearby Pennsylvania Turnpike work. The Bollingers said both sides had also agreed that the contractor would remove the topsoil, deposit the waste, and replace the soil over it. They signed without reading because they believed that obligation was included.

The contractor initially followed precisely that method, then stopped. When the owners protested, it relied on the absence of the clause from the writing. Its superintendent also said the necessary equipment had been removed. Evidence showed similar soil-restoration work on a neighbor’s property. These facts corroborated a prior shared understanding rather than merely the owners’ later preference.
sections.Procedural History: The owners sued in equity for reformation and enforcement. After hearing evidence, the trial court found mutual mistake and granted relief. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could the writing be corrected to include the topsoil obligation despite the owners’ failure to read and the contractor’s denial of a shared mistake?
sections.Holding: Yes. The evidence satisfied the substantial burden of proving that the written instrument omitted an obligation both parties had agreed upon.
sections.Reasoning:
Reformation corrects the written evidence of an agreement when it fails to reflect the parties’ actual understanding because of mutual mistake. A party’s denial after a dispute arises does not itself prevent a finding that the original omission was mutual.

The owners could not succeed simply by saying they misunderstood the document. The contractor’s initial method of performance supplied unusually strong corroboration: it did the very work the owners said was agreed upon, and it used the same method next door. The court accepted those circumstances as proof of a real omission.

The case therefore differs from an attempt to add a term to a writing that accurately records the final agreement. The accompanying notes distinguish evidence attacking a writing’s validity or accuracy—including mistake and fraud—from evidence offered to replace a valid integrated agreement with an earlier one.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It explains why the parol evidence rule does not make a mistaken writing immune from correction.

topics.parol-evidence: Evidence of a mutual drafting mistake can support reformation.
topics.mistake: Both parties’ actual agreement was omitted from the instrument.
topics.assent: Conduct corroborated the obligation the parties had agreed to.
topics.interpretation: The case concerns correcting a writing, not merely choosing among meanings of an accurate text.
topics.integration: Reformation for mutual mistake operates outside the parol evidence rule even where the writing appears to be a complete integration.
topics.notice: The Bollingers signed without reading, yet the duty-to-read rule did not defeat reformation because the omission was mutual.
